On 18 June 1995 Chernomyrdin, the chairman of the Russian government, agreed on a cessation of fighting with Shamil Basayev, the commander of the fighters of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria who had taken hostages in Budyonnovsk, a Russian-controlled town to the northwest of the republic. That evening the occupation troops halted their offensive (see: "Sham Treaties")[138]. At the end of July, Grozny, Argun, Gudermes, Shali and the mountain district centers were under occupation by the Russian army, while in most villages there were no Russian troops[138][145]. On 14 December 1995 the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Gudermes to disrupt the "vote" for the head of the puppet government. On 19-20 December, after six days of shelling and bombing of residential districts, the occupiers captured the town again[138][147].
On 17-20 February 1996 the Russian army shelled and captured by storm Novogroznensky, a settlement to the east of Gudermes[138]. On 3 March Russian troops broke into Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria, on the day their commanders had set for signing a peace with the leaders of the village, and the defenders drove the attackers out. By 9 March, after six days of shelling, the defenders of Sernovodsk were forced to leave, and the occupiers captured the village[138]. On 6 March the Armed Forces of Ichkeria under the command of Ruslan Gelayev attacked the occupiers in Grozny and liberated most of the city. The army of Ichkeria did not try to hold the city and left it on 8 March[138][145]. On the night of 14 March Russian troops surrounded Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, and on 15 March began a storming with tanks, artillery, helicopters and aircraft. On 19 March the fighters of the army of Ichkeria under the command of Khizir Khachukayev ran out of ammunition and were forced to leave[138]. On 4 April, after six days of bombing, Russian soldiers broke into Goyskoye, a village to the southwest of Grozny, but the defenders under the command of Akhmed Zakayev repelled the storming. On 7 May the occupiers under the command of General Shamanov captured Goyskoye[138]. On 24 May, after three months of stormings, shelling and bombing, the Russian army captured Bamut, a village in the west of Ichkeria at the border with Russian-controlled Ingushetia, while the defenders under the command of Ruslan Khaikhoroyev broke out of the encirclement[138].
On 9 July 1996, six days after the Russian presidential election, the occupiers violated the ceasefire agreement signed with Ichkeria on 27 May and launched a new offensive (see: "Sham Ceasefire")[138]. On that day Russian units under the command of General Tikhomirov, the commander of the occupation troops, surrounded and shelled Gekhi, a village to the southwest of Grozny, where a unit of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria was stationed. By 12 July the occupiers had killed the unit's commander Doku Makhayev and destroyed more than a third of the village[148]. On 15 July the occupiers captured Makhkety, a mountain village of the Vedeno district in the southeast of Ichkeria, which they had surrounded five days earlier[138][145].
The Russian human rights defenders of Memorial write that the Russian army with aircraft, heavy artillery and tanks fought against Ichkeria, although the president and government of Russia passed the war off as a police disarmament[138]. On 19 January 1995 the European Parliament in a resolution condemned Russia's use of the army against Ichkeria[149]. The Parliamentary Assembly of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe in a declaration of 8 July 1995 condemned Russia's war in Ichkeria as a gross violation of international law[150].
In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers. In three days of fighting the army of Ichkeria retook the center and about 80 percent of the city[145]. The defenders forced Russia to the negotiating table. On 22 August 1996 in the village of Novye Atagi in the south of the republic, Russia and Ichkeria signed an agreement on the withdrawal of Russian troops from Grozny and joint control over certain districts of the city[138][151]. On 31 August 1996 General Lebed, the secretary of the Russian Security Council, and Aslan Maskhadov, the chief of the Main Staff of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria, signed a joint statement in Khasavyurt, a town in Russian-controlled Dagestan. In it Russia acknowledged that resolving disputed issues by force or the threat of force was inadmissible (see: "Sham Treaties")[152].
By 31 August 1996 the occupation troops had left Grozny for their main bases in Khankala on the eastern outskirts of the city and at the Severny airport to the north of it. Russian police officers and soldiers of the Internal Troops of the MVD remained in the city. Russia withdrew its troops from Vedeno, Shatoy, Nozhai-Yurt and Kurchaloy, villages in the south and east of Ichkeria. Russian units still stood in Shali, near Bamut and in the Naur and Shelkovskaya districts in the north of Ichkeria[145]. In these two districts beyond the Terek river there was no fighting during the whole war. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[138].

T0025 Information Isolation
September 1994
C1193.T0025 →
C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996)
G0011 Russian Federation
S0010 Regular Army

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers bombed Chechen television, jammed journalists' satellite links and kept them away from the sites of their strikes.
Commanders of the occupation forces ordered that journalists not be let into the sites of assaults and bombings. The Russian military and police at checkpoints did not let journalists, including those with accreditation from the Russian government, into the villages and towns that Russian troops were striking (see: "Censorship")[138][153]. Human rights defenders of the American Committee to Protect Journalists write that Russian troops in Ichkeria jammed journalists' satellite transmissions, exposed their film and destroyed their equipment[154].
On 29 November 1994, Russia announced that at 2 p.m. it would cut off all communications with Ichkeria[155]. From 21 to 24 December, Russian pilots struck the television center in Grozny. Deinekin, commander of Russian military aviation, named the aim of these strikes: "to stop the rabid anti-Russian propaganda"[138].
On 3 January 1995, Russian pilots bombed Shali, a town southeast of Grozny. Human rights defenders of Human Rights Watch write that the pilots were apparently trying to hit a radio communication tower, but killed several townspeople at the market and in the hospital (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[156]. On 7 and 8 April, the Internal Troops of Russia's Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, and killed 103 Chechen civilians there (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")[157]. On 11 April, the occupiers at the post near the village did not let journalists in and admitted them only on 13 April[158][157]. On 8 October, Russian pilots bombed Roshni-Chu, a village southwest of Grozny (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). The occupiers blocked all the roads to the village, and men of the police special forces from the Russian city of Irkutsk at the post did not let journalists in, citing an order[138][159]. From 11 December, before the "elections" of the head of the puppet government on 14-17 December, Russian soldiers at checkpoints did not let journalists without special passes into Grozny (see: "Sham Expression of Popular Will")[138]. From 14 to 20 December, after the Armed Forces of Ichkeria had liberated Gudermes, the second-largest city of the republic, the occupiers shelled and bombed the city, and until 25 December did not let the press in (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[147].
In January 1996, the command of the occupation forces closed Grozny and the east of Ichkeria to the press[147]. From February until the first days of March, the occupiers shelled with artillery the encircled settlement of Novogroznensky in the east of Ichkeria and the villages of Alleroy, Tsentoroy, Bachi-Yurt and Suvorov-Yurt (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). The Russian military did not let journalists in there[138]. From 3 to 9 March, Russian troops shelled Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria, with artillery and fired on it from helicopters (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[138]. From 6 to 9 March, while the Armed Forces of Ichkeria were attacking the occupiers in Grozny, Russian officials did not let journalists into the city[154]. On 10 March, the Russian military commandant of Sernovodsk forbade letting journalists, human rights defenders and any foreigners into the village (see: "Expulsion of Foreign Missions")[138].
On 15 March 1996, the Internal Troops of Russia's Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Russian 58th Army began the assault on Samashki (see: "Military Intervention")[138]. Sources differ on the number of Chechen civilians the occupiers killed in the village during the assault: 35 according to the villagers' list[138] or about 600 according to a doctor who treated people there (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[145][153]. On 17 and 18 March, the occupiers did not let independent journalists from Moscow through to the village. Maria Eismont, a correspondent of the Moscow newspaper Segodnya, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Moscow on 22 April that on 26 and 27 March the Russian military stopped her on the roads to Samashki, and that she got into the village five days later. In Sernovodsk, Russian soldiers who had taken part in the assault turned the journalists back with the words: "There's no need to go there, there's nothing for you to do there, all the more so since there is nothing at all left to look at." Alexander Trushin, a correspondent of the Moscow newspaper Obshchaya Gazeta, told the Glasnost tribunal on 21 April that in early April the chief of the Russian checkpoint near the village phoned a general and did not let the journalists through: "I asked the captain: 'Did you report why we are going, for what purpose?' He answered: 'Yes, the general knows, and nevertheless the order is not to let you through'"[153]. Human rights defenders of Memorial write that reports of this assault did not reach television and radio[138].
On 21 April 1996, the occupiers killed Dzhokhar Dudayev, the president of Ichkeria, during his conversation on a satellite phone with a mediator in the peace talks; according to the version that human rights defenders of Memorial consider likely, the Russian military located the signal of this phone (see: "Neutralization of the Opposition")[160][138]. On 8 August 1996, while the Armed Forces of Ichkeria were liberating Grozny, Russian soldiers did not let four journalists of foreign media into the city through either of its two entrances[154].
Human rights defenders of Memorial write that in the second year of the war Russian troops cut off from the press the areas they deemed undesirable far more tightly and successfully than in the first year[138].
In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[145]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[152]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[138].

T0045.001 Destruction of Shrines and Necropolises
September 1994
C1193.T0045.001 →
C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996)
G0011 Russian Federation
S0010 Regular Army

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers destroyed mosques, shelled cemeteries and razed ancient burial mounds south of Grozny to the ground.
Russian artillerymen, pilots and helicopter crews shelled mosques in the villages and towns of Ichkeria[161][138]. Approaching a village, the occupiers first of all fired at the top of the mosque, the tallest building, and snipers fired at mosques for no reason[153]. By the estimate of Isa Adayev, director of the National Museum of Ichkeria, by May 1996 Russian troops had destroyed or damaged 70 percent of the republic's mosques[153]. Russian helicopter crews bombed village cemeteries, and snipers fired at them[156][162].
In February-March 1995, a Russian regiment stood for two months and seven days beside three ancient burial mounds, earthen hills over graves, between the villages of Starye Atagi and Chechen-Aul south of Grozny. The Grozny city council had set aside 26 hectares around the mounds for a museum of archaeology, and a fence, signs warning that these were monuments, and building materials had been brought there. Soldiers dug up the middle of the mounds with a special vehicle that accompanies tank regiments, and then razed them to the ground. The occupiers knocked down the fence and the signs with tanks. Soldiers dug trenches between the mounds and used the museum's building materials for dugouts and checkpoints. In May 1996, Isa Adayev told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Prague: "These were deliberate actions. One or two random hits could not have done what was done"[153].
In early February 1995, Russian snipers fired from the hills above Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, at the village cemetery and damaged graves. Because of the shooting, families postponed for a day the funerals of Chechens whom the occupiers had killed with mortar fire on 2 February[156]. In April 1995, Russian helicopter crews bombed Koshkeldy, a village in the east of Ichkeria, and the village cemetery[162]. From 14 to 20 December 1995, artillerymen of the occupation troops shelled the mosque in Gudermes, the second-largest town of Ichkeria, and killed more than 30 townspeople beside it (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[138].
By February 1996, Russian troops had destroyed the mosques and minarets, the towers beside mosques, in Bamut, a village in the west of Ichkeria[161].
From 3 to 9 March 1996, Russian troops stormed Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria. Russian soldiers burned the village mosque together with the bodies of Chechens whom the villagers had brought there for burial (see: "Desecration of the Dead")[163][153]. In May 1996, Sadyt Gisatova, a Chechen woman from Sernovodsk, told the Glasnost tribunal in Prague: "When we came to the mosque to bury the bodies lying there, we saw that the mosque had burned down. All the bodies had burned too. In what countries do they destroy churches and mosques? It is the holy of holies"[153].
By May 1996, the occupation troops, while bombing Grozny, had destroyed the memorial to the victims of the deportation of the Chechens to Central Asia in 1944, and had shot the inscription off the stone. Chechens had built the memorial in 1992 from gravestones that, after the deportation, the colonizers had used to build buildings, roads and pig farms[164][153].
In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[145]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[152]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[138].

T0045.002 Burning of Books and Archives
September 1994
C1193.T0045.002 →
C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996)
G0011 Russian Federation
S0010 Regular Army

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers burned the archives, libraries, books and manuscripts of the Chechens.
Russian artillerymen shelled, and pilots bombed, the buildings of the archive, libraries and research institutes in Grozny. The documents, books and manuscripts in these buildings burned[138][153]. Russian commanders, with the help of soldiers, carried ancient books away on trucks toward Mozdok, a town in North Ossetia, and toward Ingushetia, both Russian-controlled (see: "Theft of Cultural Property")[153].
From 31 December 1994, the occupation troops stormed the center of Grozny, where the Central State Archive of the Chechen Republic kept about 656 thousand files on the history of the Chechen and Ingush peoples over more than two centuries. One building of the archive stood on Ordzhonikidze Street, a hundred meters from the palace of the president of Ichkeria[138]. Oleg Orlov, a human rights defender of Memorial, who at the start of the storming was in the basement of the palace together with the group of Sergei Kovalyov, Russia's human rights commissioner, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Moscow in February 1996 that on the night of 4 January 1995 he came out of the basement: "We saw that the whole center of the city was already destroyed, practically all the residential buildings had either burned down or were still burning. … We saw that archive – it had burned down completely"[161]. In February 1995, Yeremchenko, deputy head of the Russian archival agency, came to Grozny and established that in the archive buildings on Ordzhonikidze and Chekhov streets the occupiers had destroyed all the documents together with the backup copies on film. The third building of the archive, on Karagandinskaya Street, survived. It kept about 90 thousand files on the Chechens and Ingush whom the USSR had deported to Kazakhstan in 1944. On 21 September 1995, Yeremchenko, deputy head of the agency, wrote in reply to an inquiry that the occupiers had destroyed 87 percent of the 795 thousand files in all the state archives of the Chechen Republic[138].
In early 1995, Russian troops burned down the entire Chekhov Republican Scientific Library in Grozny with shelling[138]. On 24 April 1996, the ethnographer Yan Chesnov, who studied the Chechens and saw the ruins of the library, told the public tribunal of the Glasnost Foundation in Moscow: "The archive and the republican library have been burned. … The entire book collection has been burned. Books in the Chechen language published in the 1930s in Latin script [in Latin letters], ancient Arabic books. A unique library has perished"[153].
In January 1995, the occupiers destroyed the Chechen National Museum in Grozny with shelling, together with its department of ancient books and manuscripts (see: "Destruction of Historical Memory")[153]. In early 1995, Russian troops destroyed in Grozny the library of the Research Institute of the Humanities of the Chechen Republic. The library kept the works of all the known researchers of the Caucasus, the records of expeditions on the languages of the Chechens and Ingush, and the originals of medieval books and manuscripts[138].
Human rights defenders of Memorial write that in Grozny the scientific and technical library, three university libraries, the libraries of all the research institutes, the republican children's library and the archives of the unions of writers, artists, composers and theater workers burned down. According to Memorial, the occupiers destroyed or irreparably damaged the folklore center with its archive[138].
In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[145]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[152]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[138].

T0045 Destruction of Historical Memory
September 1994
C1193.T0045 →
C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996)
G0011 Russian Federation
S0010 Regular Army

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers destroyed the museums, research institutes and ancient monuments of the Chechens.
During the storming of Grozny, Russian artillerymen shelled, and pilots bombed, the center of the city, where the museums and research institutes of Ichkeria stood[138][153]. Russian pilots fired rockets at ancient towers and settlements in the mountains in the south of Ichkeria[153]. The occupiers occupied the ruins of museums and looted what had survived (see: "Theft of Cultural Property")[153]. Russian troops burned almost the entire Central State Archive of the Chechen Republic and the republican libraries in Grozny (see: "Burning of Books and Archives")[138]. Soldiers of the occupation troops destroyed mosques and leveled ancient burial mounds (see: "Destruction of Shrines and Necropolises")[153].
In January 1995, Russian troops destroyed the Chechen National Museum in Grozny. The museum held about 320 thousand exhibits, among them archaeological finds of the ancient and medieval Caucasus, traditional Chechen clothing and old manuscripts[138][153]. The museum's director Isa Adayev told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Prague in May 1996: "From 1 to 4 January 1995, the museum building was shelled quite deliberately from several directions". When the director got to the museum on 7 January, "it was no longer a museum — nothing was left of it — only ruins". On 18 January, Russian special forces seized the ruins[153]. Khotin, deputy director of the museum center of the Russian Ministry of Culture, who inspected the ruins of the museum in late March 1995, told the public tribunal of the Glasnost Foundation in Moscow in February 1996: "The nature of the destruction shows that barrage fire was used there. Next to the museum there is a small park of about 50 fairly old trees. Well, all those trees are cut in half. All of them!"[161].
In early 1995, the occupiers destroyed in Grozny the Research Institute of the Humanities of the Chechen Republic, founded in 1907[138]. In 1995, Russian pilots fired rockets at and bombed Kogo-Maista, an old settlement in the mountains in the south of Ichkeria, far from the fighting. In the strikes, the occupiers destroyed six towers that had stood for thirteen centuries, killed the Chechen boy Deni Murtazov and wounded a woman of his family so badly that she became disabled[153].
The human rights defenders of "Memorial" write that Russian troops destroyed or irreparably damaged in Grozny the university, the pedagogical and petroleum institutes, and the geological museum. In "Memorial's" assessment, Russian troops did not take the rescue of cultural property into account and inflicted irreparable damage on the culture of the Chechen people[138].
In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[145]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[152]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[138].

T0053 Abduction of People
September 1994
C1193.T0053 →
C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996)
G0011 Russian Federation
S0010 Regular Army

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers abducted Chechens and concealed information about their fate, whereabouts or condition from their relatives.
Russian servicemen, fighters of OMON (police special forces) and of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) detained Chechens at checkpoints and led them away from their homes, sometimes at night[165][138][161]. Russian soldiers checked passports against arrest lists, which they received from the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs, detained Chechens by them even with documents and passes, and then handed them over to the headquarters of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs in Ichkeria. Women and old people also ended up on these lists[153].
Russian servicemen and police officers did not let detained Chechens inform their families about themselves, and their relatives considered them missing. The occupiers put the abducted in pits at military units and did not register the arrest (see: "Filtration Camp System")[138][161].
The Russian military transported detained Chechens from commandant's offices to filtration camps, and on the way people often disappeared without a trace. When relatives found out where a person was being held, the Russian guards immediately moved him elsewhere[153].
To inquiries about missing people who appeared on the lists of the filtration camps, Russian agencies replied that these people had been released[138]. The Chechen society "Victims of War" searched for Chechens whom the occupiers had detained in Grozny and at checkpoints from 11 December 1994 to May 1995, and did not find a single one of them on the Russian list of 252 released. At the addresses from the Russian lists, the women of the society found no people with such surnames[153].
Relatives of the missing filed statements with the society "Victims of War". As of 8 August 1995, 1308 peaceful citizens of Ichkeria were listed as missing[138]. By mid-October 1996, the society's list held 1432 missing Chechens[166]. In the spring of 1997, Ichkeria handed Russia a list of 1563 missing[138].
The Russian military tortured and killed some of the abducted, and relatives later found their bodies where Russian units had been stationed (see: "Killing of Prisoners and Detainees")[138].
On 9 January 1995, the occupiers detained Shamsa Magomadov in Grozny, and the guards of the filtration camp in Mozdok, a town in Russian-controlled North Ossetia, recorded that they had released him on 2 February[153]. Shamsa Magomadov did not return home, and in the winter of 1995-1996 the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs promised his sister to exchange her brother for a captured Russian soldier (see: "Hostage-Taking")[153][138]. On 21 May 1995, at checkpoint No. 13 near Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, the Russian military detained Ruslan Parshoev from that village, and the Russian major Morozov took him to his unit near Assinovskaya, a stanitsa in the west of Ichkeria. The next day, Lvov, the chief of staff of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs in Ichkeria, ordered the detainee sent to Khankala, the main base of the occupation troops on the eastern outskirts of Grozny, where he was taken by fighters of the "Rus" special forces unit, and Ruslan Parshoev went missing[138]. In the summer of 1995, the occupiers abducted at a checkpoint on the road to Grozny Khamad Kurbanov, the representative of the president of Ichkeria in Russia, who had just been released after a month without charge in a Moscow prison[167]. Russian guards held Khamad Kurbanov in a pit near Assinovskaya and in the filtration camp in Grozny until a commission under the international OSCE mission secured his release at the negotiations between Russia and Ichkeria[153]. On 23 December 1995, the Russian military, working from lists, took Ruslan Soslambekov, chairman of the movement "People's Diplomacy for Peace and Unity", at a checkpoint at the entrance to Grozny, kept him for 28 days in the filtration camp on the outskirts of the city, then released him[161].
In February 1996, the Russian military stopped at checkpoints 26 acquaintances of Madina Magomadova from the society "Victims of War", and all of them disappeared[153].
At dawn on 1 August 1996, OMON fighters of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs in helicopters, jeeps and armored personnel carriers attacked the settlement of Dolinsky north-west of Grozny[168]. Movla Idrisov from Dolinsky told a Reuters correspondent on the day of the raid that the OMON men went into the first and second floors, led away all the men they found, and left one: a 65-year-old with one leg, on crutches[169]. The urgent action of Amnesty International of 6 August 1996 says that the OMON men led away 18 Chechens, among them Aslanbek Gassayev and Umakh Mogamedov: "The men were led with sacks over their heads to a waiting bus and driven away. They have not been seen since"[168]. In 1996, the UN Working Group on Enforced Disappearances requested from Russia information on the fate of two of them, and in 1997 Russia replied that their cases were being investigated by the Prosecutor General's Office, the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the FSB[170][171].
On 24 August 1996, eight Russian soldiers led away from a yard in Grozny Aleksei Karmayev, a 67-year-old disabled man who had complained to the headquarters of the 276th Regiment of the Russian army about looting, after which the disabled man went missing[166][172].
By the end of October 1996, the prison department of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs replied to a list of more than 1300 missing, handed over after the ceasefire in June 1996, that forty people from the list had been held in custody and released, but all forty had been released before 1993, before the war. About the rest the department said nothing. On 22 January 1997, Izmailov, an officer of the Russian search group, said on air on the ORT television channel that the missing Chechens were most likely no longer alive, and did not specify whether the Russian military had killed them in battle or shot them on detention, or whether they had died in custody[166]. In January 1998, the UN Working Group on Enforced Disappearances reported that Russia had not clarified the fate of a single missing person about whom it had been asked[171].
On 10 June 1996, the working groups of Russia and Ichkeria on the search for the missing agreed to stop detentions based on lists and other papers without legal force[173].
In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[145]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[152]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[138].

T0099 Hostage-Taking
September 1994
C1193.T0099 →
C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996)
G0011 Russian Federation
S0010 Regular Army

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers took peaceful Chechens hostage and released them in exchange for captured and killed Russian servicemen, weapons or money.
Russian servicemen drew up lists of detained Chechens for exchange and put on them people who by their age could not have carried weapons[153]. According to a certificate by the prison service of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs, from 11 December 1994 to 22 July 1995 the ministry handed over 141 prisoners of the filtration camps for exchange for captured Russian servicemen (see: "Filtration Camp System")[138].
Russian police officers and soldiers promised to release a detained Chechen if his relatives brought money, a Russian soldier out of captivity or the body of a dead one[138][153]. The occupiers used the hostages' relatives to find out where the Armed Forces of Ichkeria were holding captured Russians: the relatives searched for captives to rescue their own, while the Russian FSB collected information from them and on 29 July 1995 drew up a certificate on the places where Russian soldiers were being held[138][174].
On 9 January 1995, Russian servicemen detained Shamsu Magomadov in Grozny (see: "Abduction of People"). In the winter of 1995-1996, his sister Madina Magomadova sought her brother's exchange from Colonel Pilyugin of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs. She told "Memorial": "They told me: 'Yes, your brother is alive, we will exchange him — find a soldier [a captured Russian soldier]'. I found a soldier — I went through all those mountains, villages, there is a war on, under fire I searched for a soldier — I found one, brought a photograph. They tell me: 'The soldier is a deserter, he is not subject to exchange…' … 'Go find an officer'. … I found an officer, brought a photograph of the officer... They tell me: sorry, Comrade Magomadova, your brother has been taken away from here, and where he is supposed to be, he has not been brought yet. We cannot find him". The occupiers never released Shamsu Magomadov, and nothing is known of his fate[138].
Russian servicemen and security services put up for exchange the captured relatives and guards of the president of Ichkeria. On 19 February 1995, the occupiers detained in Grozny Makharbi Dudayev, the president's younger brother, and on 6 April the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs put him up for exchange in Malye Atagi, a village south of Grozny, together with 16 prisoners of the filtration camps. The ministry exchanged the prisoners for a captured Russian major and released the president's brother separately[138][143][158]. On the night of 28 May 1996, Russian border guards detained the widow of the president of Ichkeria with her bodyguard at the airport of Nalchik, the capital of Russian-controlled Kabardino-Balkaria, and the Russian FSB released the widow but exchanged the bodyguard for a captured Russian priest[175][176].
Russian soldiers and filtration camp guards demanded ransom for detained Chechens. In late March 1995, the guards of the military unit near Assinovskaya, a stanitsa in the west of Ichkeria, asked detained Chechens who would pay more to get out[138]. In April 1995, the guards of the filtration camp on the northeastern outskirts of Grozny received five million rubles for the release of a detained Chechen[161]. On 15 May 1995, Russian soldiers put a detained Chechen from Shali, a town southeast of Grozny, into a pit at their unit, offered to let him out for money and released him after 18 hours[165]. In December 1995, Russian servicemen detained five elderly Chechens at a checkpoint, and their relatives ransomed them from a filtration camp for ten million rubles[161]. On 17 April 1996, Russian soldiers detained a Chechen woman with her two brothers at the entrance to Grozny and demanded three million rubles for them, and in the evening released all three, and the brother gave them the money[153]. On 18 April, Russian servicemen took six Chechens from their homes in Novye Aldy, a settlement on the southwestern outskirts of Grozny, and their relatives ransomed them from the filtration camp at the city motor depot[153].
The Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs and the command of the occupation troops demanded captured Russian servicemen, their bodies and weapons for detained Chechens. In March 1996, officers of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs demanded that the female relatives of a Chechen, held since January in the filtration camp in Grozny, dig up and bring the bodies of three officers of a Russian police special unit, and in late March, having received the bodies, released him[138]. In March 1996, soldiers of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs detained three Chechens at the checkpoint between Goity and Starye Atagi, villages south of Grozny, and on 28 March the occupiers exchanged them for five Russian soldiers[166]. On 7 April 1996, Russian servicemen took Saidash Shamakhurov from Gikalovo, a village south of Grozny, to Khankala, the main base of the occupation troops on the eastern outskirts of Grozny, where investigators demanded that he record on tape his request to be exchanged for 15 captured Russian soldiers and 48 construction workers. On 27 April, the occupiers exchanged him for a Russian soldier[166]. In May 1996, soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) detained in the center of Grozny 17 to 20 Chechens who were repairing heating pipes and demanded during interrogation that their relatives bring weapons or captured Russian servicemen for them. The next evening the guards let them go[166].
Russian soldiers took hostages during assaults and when encircled. On 7 April 1995, during the storming of Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, the occupiers took four Chechen men hostage, drove them into a pit in a garage and fired at them with assault rifles. One the occupiers killed on the spot, the wounded second one the next day; two survived (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")[138]. On 10-12 August 1996, soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs, encircled by the Armed Forces of Ichkeria, held about 500 patients, their relatives and medics hostage in City Hospital No. 9 in Grozny. On 12 August, the occupiers left the hospital, taking a hundred hostages as a human shield, and released them near the former driving school where Russian units were stationed, once the defenders had handed over four captured Russian soldiers (see: "Use of People as "Human Shields"")[143][138].
On 11 and 12 August 1996, when the Armed Forces of Ichkeria were liberating Grozny from the occupiers, soldiers of the 101st Brigade of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs took Chechen men from the blocks around the "15th Gorodok", their base on Lenin Street, and held them there as hostages. On 14 October 1996, Magomed Taramov told "Memorial" how on 12 August Russian servicemen took him from his home together with his son Alimkhan: "We are no 'boyeviki' [as Russians called the Armed Forces of Ichkeria], we took no part in the armed actions. They led us out into the street, and there by the wall stood another nine or so people... In all, about twenty-four of us were gathered". For the release of the hostages, the brigade's officers demanded that relatives bring wounded soldiers from the encircled Russian checkpoints and the bodies of the dead, or get the army of Ichkeria to let food through to those posts. Garib Asiyalov, whom the hostages' female relatives called to the talks at the "15th Gorodok", in October told "Memorial" the words of a Russian officer: "…I answer to Kulikov [the head of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs]. We will trade head for head — our wounded or dead one for your living one". According to him, for the wounded and dead soldiers whom the relatives brought by truck, the brigade released 32 hostages[143]. On 16 August, when relatives brought the bodies of eight Russian servicemen to the base, the occupiers released Magomed and Alimkhan Taramov[138].
On 17 August 1996, soldiers of the 101st Brigade searched the blocks near the "15th Gorodok" and took Chechen men from there to the base as hostages. The brigade's officers promised to release them for the bodies of Russian soldiers buried near the bus station and the chemical plant, and on 19 August, when Russian soldiers brought 28 bodies out through the positions of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria, they released the hostages. The human rights defenders of "Memorial" published the names of twelve of them[143] and write that at the "15th Gorodok" and in City Hospital No. 9 in Grozny the soldiers of the Internal Troops took hostages on the direct orders of the commanders of their units[138].
In his report of 26 March 1996, the UN Secretary-General cited reports by human rights organizations: Russian troops often detained any Chechen man, whether there was evidence against him or not, in order to exchange him for captured Russian soldiers[177]. The human rights defenders of "Memorial" write that Russian agencies repeatedly used civilian prisoners of the filtration camps as hostages and in most cases offered Ichkeria in exchange Chechens who had not taken part in the fighting. In "Memorial's" conclusion, hostage-taking became a regular practice for the Russian military[138].
Russian prosecutors put none of the occupiers who took hostages in Hospital No. 9 and at the "15th Gorodok" in Grozny on trial (see: "Impunity of Perpetrators")[166][138].
In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[145]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[152]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[138].

T0104 Mass Killings of Civilians
September 1994
C1193.T0104 →
C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996)
G0011 Russian Federation
S0010 Regular Army

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers killed unarmed Chechens on the roads, in houses and in cellars.
In the captured villages and towns Russian soldiers together with police officers went from house to house during "zachistkas" ("sweeps", as the Russians called the house searches and detentions of Chechens). The occupiers threw grenades into cellars where families were hiding from the shelling. Russian soldiers set houses on fire together with the people inside. Against the walls of houses the occupiers shot unarmed Chechens, among them women and old people[138]. Russian snipers fired at those who came out of houses and cellars. Under sniper fire Chechen families could not collect the bodies of their relatives from the streets and bury them for several days[147][178].
On 17 December 1994 the Russian military fired from armored personnel carriers at a column of refugees from Grozny at the border with Russian-controlled Ingushetia and killed ten people on the spot[138]. On 22 December 1994 a Russian pilot bombed the cars that had gathered at a crossroads in Grozny, and then fired two more rockets at those who ran to help the wounded. In all, the occupiers killed up to twenty people at the crossroads[138][161].
In early January 1995 special forces of the 67th Brigade of Russian military intelligence blocked a mountain road along which Chechen civilians were leaving Grozny to escape the shelling. The intelligence troops called in attack aircraft, and Russian pilots bombed the refugees' cars that had gathered at the roadblock[138]. In Shali, a town to the southeast of Grozny, on 3 January 1995 Russian pilots dropped cluster bombs on the car market and bombed a second time those who ran to help the wounded (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[138][161]. Russian servicemen who were searching yards in the settlement of Butenko on the outskirts of Grozny shot four people with assault rifles on 29 January and 3 February 1995, among them three members of the Gagayev family[161][138]. OMON officers, SOBR fighters (police special forces) and soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian MVD (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) searched houses in Petropavlovskaya, a stanitsa to the northeast of Grozny, on 3 February and killed five Chechens[153].
In early March 1995 the Armed Forces of Ichkeria, at the insistence of the villagers, were forced to leave Samashki, a village in the west of the Chechen Republic. On 7 April, after shelling, about 250 soldiers of the Sofrino Brigade of the Internal Troops of the Russian MVD, OMON officers and SOBR fighters from Moscow, the Moscow region and Orenburg stormed the village. The occupiers captured Samashki after a short fight with a small group of armed Chechens from the village[157][138]. In the evening Russian soldiers drove four men who were hiding in a storeroom into a car-repair pit in a garage and shot them with assault rifles. The occupiers killed 71-year-old Musait Isayev and wounded Nasruddin Bazuyev and Salavdi Umakhanov, while Abdurakhman Chindigayev survived. Salavdi Umakhanov told Oleg Orlov of Memorial on 4 August 1995: "Musa [Musait Isayev] says: 'Guys, don't shoot. The cattle have to be fed... Don't shoot'… In an instant they gave him a burst of automatic fire from there." The next day the Russian military killed the wounded Nasruddin Bazuyev and his daughter Raisa Masayeva[138].
On 8 April, when no one in the village was resisting any longer, soldiers, OMON officers and SOBR fighters searched the houses. Sadulla Yusupov, an elderly Chechen from Samashki, told Oleg Orlov of Memorial on 13 April: "At ten in the morning soldiers came running here… They were screaming in inhuman voices, swearing, cursing, shouting: 'Come out, you bitches!' and they went up to every house and fired." A Russian soldier fired an assault rifle into the earthen cellar where he had hidden, and a second occupier threw a grenade in and wounded him. When he climbed out, Sadulla Yusupov saw the bodies of six neighbors on the street, among them two old men and a woman[138]. The Russian military shot Lechi Arsayev dead from twenty meters, without trying to detain him, as he was hanging a white flag on the fence of his house. On Sharipov Street Russian soldiers set fire to a house where Chechens were hiding. The occupiers immediately shot Abi Akhmetova, who came out of the fire with her hands raised. The report of the Observer Mission of Russian human rights organizations says that Yuki Gaitukayeva, Madu Rasuyev and Kesirt Rasuyeva could not get out of the burning house and apparently burned alive[157]. The mission published a list by name of 103 people whom the occupiers killed in Samashki on 7 and 8 April[157]. The human rights defenders of Memorial write that at least half of them the Russian military killed deliberately[138].
On 23 April 1995 drunken Russian servicemen opened fire near a shop in the center of Gudermes, the second-largest town of Ichkeria, and soldiers of other Russian units took it for an attack and fired in the town for three and a half hours. By the count of the prosecutor's office that Russia had installed in Grozny, the occupiers killed ten unarmed people that day and wounded eight[138]. On 7 July 1995, during the talks between Russia and Ichkeria, the Russian military killed seven Chechens of the Chapanov family, among them children and old people, in Prigorodnoye, a village near Grozny[138]. From 15 December 1995 the crews of Russian helicopters fired at Chechens who were leaving Gudermes to escape the shelling. On the road to the east of the town the pilots killed or wounded about fifteen people[138][147]. On 19-20 December 1995, having again captured Gudermes, which the Armed Forces of Ichkeria had liberated five days earlier, Russian soldiers went around the houses and threw grenades into cellars where old, sick and wounded people were hiding. Shkirko, the commander of the occupation troops, named 267 civilians killed in Gudermes (see: "Lies about Its Own Actions")[138].
On 3 March 1996 Russian soldiers who broke into Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria, fired from an armored personnel carrier at three men in a car, killing them and wounding a fourth[138]. On 17 March, during the second storming of Samashki, Russian soldiers led about 40 Chechens, among them 10-15 children, out of a cellar in a yard on Kalinin Street and stood them against a wall. After going out of the gate, the occupiers threw three grenades into the yard and wounded 17 people, two women among them dying of their wounds[138][153]. On 19 March Russian soldiers led the Chechens hiding in the cellars of one of the yards of Samashki out and lined them up against a wall. With a burst of automatic fire the occupiers killed Zakhud Zhadiyeva, a Chechen woman who did not understand the order "stand against the wall" in Russian[153]. On 25 April 1996 soldiers from a Russian checkpoint fired at buses in which women and children were being taken out of the surrounded Shali. The occupiers wounded nine people, one woman among them dying of her wounds[138][179]. On the night of 15 July 1996 in the northwestern suburb of Grozny, soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian MVD fired from two armored personnel carriers at unarmed people in cars and killed 12 or 13 people. The occupiers set the cars on fire and cut off the ears of some of the bodies (see: "Desecration of the Dead")[148][138]. On 1 August OMON officers of the Russian MVD attacked the settlement of Dolinsky to the northwest of Grozny and shot dead two young men who were sleeping in a car near the houses (see: "Abduction of People")[168]. On 10 August Russian soldiers who were capturing the area of Abakanskaya Street in Grozny fired flamethrowers into the cellars of houses without checking whether there were people inside. In the cellar of house No. 40 the occupiers burned 12 Chechens from two families, among them two children aged three and four and an 85-year-old woman[138]. On 19 August 1996 the command of the occupation troops demanded that everyone who remained in Grozny leave the city within 48 hours (see: "Collective Punishment"). The next day near the village of Goity to the south of Grozny the crew of a Russian helicopter fired at refugees who were leaving the capital in buses and cars, and killed from ten to twelve people[138][180].
Memorial concluded that Russian troops deliberately attacked civilians throughout the war and killed the most of them by bombing and shelling[138]. Tim Guldimann, the head of the mission of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe in Grozny, wrote that in March 1996 his staff, in a report to the organization's leadership, called Russia's actions a war against the civilian population without military necessity[181].
The human rights defenders of Memorial write that Russia kept no count of the unarmed Chechens it killed[138]. The Observer Mission questioned 265 refugee families from Grozny and, based on their accounts, estimated that from December 1994 to March 1995 the occupiers killed 25,000-29,000 people in the city[138]. In March 1996 the UN Secretary-General, in a report to the UN Commission on Human Rights, cited the calculation of Russian human rights organizations: from 25 November 1994 to 15 April 1995, 26,550 civilians died in Ichkeria from Russia's war, among them 2,300 children under 15 and 5,050 women[177]. In its annual report for 1996 Human Rights Watch estimated the number of civilians killed in Ichkeria since December 1994 at 18,500 to 80,000[180].
Over the whole war Russian military courts convicted seven servicemen for the killing of civilians (see: "Impunity of Perpetrators")[138].
In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[145]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[152]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[138].

T0105 Total Destruction of Infrastructure
September 1994
C1193.T0105 →
C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996)
G0011 Russian Federation
S0010 Regular Army

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers destroyed the towns and villages of Ichkeria together with their housing, hospitals and schools[138].
Russian pilots and artillerymen destroyed residential neighborhoods with bombing and shelling (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[138]. In captured villages and towns, Russian soldiers and police officers looted houses (see: "Pillage") and then set them on fire with gasoline, hay or flamethrowers[157][162][153]. After the war of 1994-1996, 60,000 families of Grozny were left without housing[182].
The occupiers destroyed substations, tore down power lines and blew up gas pipelines[161][153].
In December 1994, Russian aviation bombed Grozny, the capital of Ichkeria. On 9 January 1995, Irina from the Third Microdistrict on the outskirts of Grozny told Human Rights Watch in Russian-controlled Ingushetia: "Our region was the first to suffer… either December 17th or 18th, three nine-story apartment buildings of the institute 'Promavtomatika' were bombed out. People all become homeless"[183]. On the night of 20 December, Russian pilots dropped two bombs on a block of one-story houses at the intersection of Moskovskaya Street and Noya Buachidze Street and completely or partially destroyed 18 houses[138]. Russian aviation bombed a substation, and Grozny was left without electricity[161]. On 31 December 1994, the occupiers began the assault on the city. After 20 February 1995, Russian special forces set fire to and blew up houses in Grozny and destroyed pipes and power lines[153]. More than two months after the start of the assault, by 6 March 1995, Russian troops had captured Grozny. On 1 May 1995, the Russian journalist Yevgenia Albats, who had been in the city in January, said at a hearing of a commission of the US Congress: "There is no such city any more. There isn't a single house in Grozny that hasn't been destroyed one way or another by the war"[184].
On 3 February 1995, soldiers of the Russian OMON (police special forces) and of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) searched houses in Petropavlovskaya, a stanitsa northeast of Grozny, and burned 14 houses. In all, the occupiers destroyed 86 houses in the stanitsa[153]. In February 1995, Russian pilots bombed two schools, a sports school, a hospital and a kindergarten in Argun, a town east of Grozny[156]. At the end of March 1995, Russian troops captured Gudermes, the second-largest city of Ichkeria, without a fight, and on 29 and 30 March soldiers burned houses in it with flamethrowers; on Parkhomenko Street two houses were left intact[138][162]. In April 1995, Russian troops shelled for a month Alleroy, a village in the east of Ichkeria with 4,500-5,000 inhabitants. The occupiers completely destroyed a fifth of the houses of Alleroy with rockets[138].
On 7 April 1995, the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs and the OMON stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria. Chechens in Samashki told observers of the Russian human rights organization "Memorial" that the soldiers and OMON men burned houses on 8 April, when they were searching the village. Russian servicemen spent the night in the school on Kooperativnaya Street, and in the morning set it on fire, and the school burned out from the inside[157]. On 10 April, a Chechen woman named Karnukayeva from Rabochaya Street told the Observer Mission of Russian human rights organizations: "The houses are burned. I have nowhere to go now. I am left on the street hungry and cold with 4 children"[157]. Viktor Lozinsky of "Memorial" examined the burned houses of Samashki from 18 April to 1 May 1995. In February 1996, he told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation: "The village was being burned out systematically. The houses were set on fire like this: a window was broken with a rifle butt, and wiping cloth [rags] soaked in some diesel fuel was simply put on the windowsill and set alight"[161]. The Observer Mission published a list drawn up by the administration of Samashki of 198 yards where the occupiers had completely destroyed at least one house, and in 155 of them almost all the houses had burned down[157]. The human rights defenders of "Memorial" write that the Russian military and officers of the Ministry of Internal Affairs burned most of the houses in the village deliberately[138].
From 30 September 1995 to March 1996, Russian Internal Troops and police kept Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria, encircled, tore down the power lines near the village and blew up the gas pipeline several times (see: "Transport Blockade")[153]. In December 1995, after the Armed Forces of Ichkeria had liberated Gudermes, Russian troops shelled and bombed the city. According to refugees and journalists' estimates, the occupiers destroyed or damaged about 40 percent of the buildings of Gudermes[147].
From 3 to 9 March 1996, Russian troops stormed Sernovodsk, burned or destroyed 30 percent of the houses of the village, and Russian soldiers set fire to the apartments of refugees on the northern outskirts of the village with hand-held flamethrowers[153]. On 15 March 1996, 11 months after the first assault, Russian troops stormed Samashki again and razed to the ground the House of Culture and the school, which the Chechens had rebuilt. Journalists who came after the assault saw only three surviving houses in the whole village[153]. On 3 and 4 April 1996, Russian pilots bombed Shalazhi, a village in the southwest of Ichkeria, and destroyed dozens of houses, the whole upper part of the village[138][153]. On 6 April 1996, Russian troops captured Zhani-Vedeno, a mountain village of 38 yards in the southeast of Ichkeria, from which the Chechens had fled the shelling, and for a month let no one near it. When the Russian servicemen left, one intact house remained in the village, and in place of most of the houses an observer of "Memorial" found ashes with no traces of shells or bombs[138]. From 9 to 11 July 1996, Russian artillery shelled and aviation bombed Gekhi, a village southwest of Grozny. A correspondent of the Moscow newspaper Izvestia wrote that the occupiers had destroyed more than a third of the village[138][148]. On the night of 11 July, Russian artillerymen shelled Makhkety, a mountain village in the southeast of Ichkeria, with the Grad and Uragan multiple rocket launchers, which cannot fire with precision, and destroyed 150 houses[138][148]. From 6 to 22 August 1996, Russian troops shelled Grozny with heavy artillery and bombed it, and on 21 August Russian pilots dropped incendiary bombs on the blocks of five-story buildings on Saikhanov and Ulyanov Streets, from which the buildings burned out from the inside[138]. The bulletin of the International Committee of the Red Cross of 2 September 1996 says that after the August strikes all 80,000 people in Grozny were left without electricity and medical care: all the hospitals of the city were destroyed or badly damaged[185].
On 26 July 1995, the UN Human Rights Committee, in its comments on Russia, expressed regret that the Russian armed forces had destroyed schools, hospitals and other civilian buildings[186].
In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[145]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[152]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[138].

T0111 Use of People as “Human Shields”
September 1994
C1193.T0111 →
C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996)
G0011 Russian Federation
S0010 Regular Army

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers shielded themselves with peaceful Chechens from the fire of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria.
Russian soldiers led Chechens out of the basements where they were hiding from shelling, took men from their homes and seized doctors and patients in a hospital. The occupiers put them on armored vehicles or placed them in front of themselves so that the soldiers of the army of Ichkeria would not shoot[138][166]. Russian servicemen threatened to burn or shoot the captured Chechens if the defenders fired or did not hand over captives[143]. Russian soldiers released some Chechens from the human shield after a few hours and took others to their bases. There the occupiers put them in pits and beat them (see: "Torture and Abuse")[143].
On 6-8 March 1996, when the army of Ichkeria encircled Russian checkpoint No. 6 in Grozny, an officer of the Russian commandant's office of the city advised the soldiers at the checkpoint over the radio to seize a couple of Chechen families and shield themselves with them. The soldiers at the post did not do so[187][138][188].
From 15 March 1996, the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) and the Russian 58th Army stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria (see: "Military Intervention")[138]. On 17 March, Russian soldiers drove Chechens out of the basement of a house on Rabochaya Street, where they were hiding from shelling. A major, the commander of a Russian unit, forced three women and the three Kireyev boys - aged five, eleven and twelve - to climb onto an armored vehicle[138][143]. Leila Gaerbekova, one of the three women on the vehicle, told the human rights defender Andrei Mironov on 4 May 1996: "At gunpoint they put us on a tank [an armored vehicle] on Rabochaya Street. Three children, their mother Koka, me and my sister Anya Gaerbekova. <...> They placed us in front of the tank and said: 'If a single bullet comes from over there, we will burn you'. And there were no bullets from over there, nothing". The soldiers placed almost everyone who had been hiding in the basement in front of the vehicle and led them at gunpoint for about 300 meters, to the canal in the middle of the village. Between 12 and 2 p.m., the major told the Chechens to disperse. Khizir Khachukayev, the commander of the unit of the army of Ichkeria in Samashki, told the human rights defenders of "Memorial" that his soldiers did not fire at the armored vehicles with people on them and were forced to retreat, and put up their main resistance in the center of the village once the occupiers had let the people out of the human shield[138][143].
On 15 March 1996, in Samashki, Russian soldiers led two elderly Chechens, the owner of a house on Vygonnaya Street and his neighbor, out of the house, put them on top of an armored vehicle and drove them around under bullets for six or seven hours. After nine in the evening, the occupiers' commander let both of them go[143].
On 10 August 1996, when the Armed Forces of Ichkeria were liberating Grozny, soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs searched City Hospital No. 9 in Grozny. For two days, the occupiers held about 500 patients, their relatives, doctors and nurses hostage (see: "Hostage-Taking"). Movsar Tembulatov, the deputy chief physician, told the human rights defenders of "Memorial" and Human Rights Watch in the hospital on 13 October 1996 how Russian soldiers went down into the basement: "they put me or one of the other doctors in front as some kind of cover, with a submachine gunner behind"[143][138].
On 12 August 1996, soldiers of the army of Ichkeria repelled an attack by Russian troops trying to break through to the occupiers encircled in the hospital. The commander of the Russian servicemen in the hospital agreed to lead his soldiers out in exchange for captives and demanded 100 doctors, nurses, walking patients and their relatives as a human shield for himself. Khadis Malsagov, one of the hostages, told the human rights defenders of "Memorial" on 24 August 1996: "As soon as everyone had moved away from the hospital, they [the Russian soldiers] line the women up and say they will shoot them if the captives are not handed over to them immediately". The soldiers of Khizir Khachukayev handed over all the captives. At the gates of their base, the occupiers released the people from the human shield. When the people were returning to the hospital, Russian troops fired several dozen mortar shells at it, killed the nurse Toita Kutukhanova and wounded two nurses, two doctors and a woman patient (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). On the evening of 12 August and the morning of 13 August, the patients and medics left the hospital for the building of the International Committee of the Red Cross nearby[143][138].
On 12 August 1996, soldiers of the 101st Brigade of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs took men from the blocks of Grozny around the "15th Gorodok", their base on Lenin Street, and shielded themselves with them on the way there (see: "Hostage-Taking")[138]. Two of them, a father and son, the occupiers tied with wire to an armored personnel carrier, drove under fire to Khankala, the main base of the occupation troops on the eastern outskirts of the city, and released on 16 August[143].
The 1996 report of "Memorial" says that Russian servicemen and officers of Russian agencies in Ichkeria systematically took hostages and shielded themselves with human shields. According to the report, the occupiers shielded themselves with Chechens during the last six months of the war, from March to August 1996, most often the soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs[143].
The prosecutors of the Russian army did not investigate how Russian troops shielded themselves with Chechens during assaults and held no one accountable for it (see: "Impunity of Perpetrators")[166][138].
In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[145]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[152]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[138].

T0112 Theft of Cultural Property
September 1994
C1193.T0112 →
C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996)
G0011 Russian Federation
S0010 Regular Army

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russian servicemen looted museums and the homes of Chechens in Grozny, and specialists of the Russian ministry of culture took the most valuable of the surviving paintings from the ruins to Moscow.
From 1 to 4 January 1995, the occupiers shelled the building that housed the Chechen National Museum and the Museum of Fine Arts, and burned both museums almost completely (see: "Destruction of Historical Memory")[138].
Until the spring of 1995, Russian servicemen let none of the Chechens into the ruins of the museums and plundered what had survived. The occupiers took exhibits as trophies, according to rank and position[153].
Russian soldiers loaded exhibits of the National Museum onto armored personnel carriers[153]. Commanders of the occupation troops, with the help of soldiers, took more than one truckload of ancient books from the museum's manuscript department toward Mozdok, a town in North Ossetia, and Ingushetia, both under Russian control[153].
In February 1995, officers of the FSK (a predecessor of today's FSB) packed paintings and other works of art from the ruins into a 20-ton railway container[138]. At the end of March, the Russian ministry for emergency situations brought five specialists from the Russian ministry of culture and Moscow museums to Grozny. The group catalogued the works from the container[161]. Khotin, deputy director of the ministry of culture's museum center and one of the five, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Moscow in February 1996: "We tried to carry out of the ruins everything that could be carried out. At the same time, the state of preservation of the works was practically zero. … We conserved, made presentable and took away about 60 works of fine art"[161]. Isa Adayev, director of the National Museum, told this tribunal in Prague in May 1996: "The art experts who came from Moscow helped to steal things, picking out what they wanted by degree of significance. These experts left behind what they called 'useless junk'"[153].
In 1995, during the capture of Grozny, Russian soldiers twice looted the home library of the Chechen journalist Aslan Dukaev in the city, and his sister saved only a few books[189]. In 1995, after the capture of Grozny, servicemen of unit 3111 of the Dzerzhinsky Division of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) searched the house of a Chechen on the outskirts of the city and took away a collection of ancient manuscripts, books and icons that Mikhail Patalov, a former deputy director of the Grozny Philharmonic, kept there. His complaint passed through eleven levels of the prosecutor's office, the prosecutors opened a case, but it went nowhere[138].
In July 1995, the delegation of Ichkeria at the talks with Russia in Grozny demanded the return of the National Museum's exhibits. The Russian delegation verbally promised to look into it[153]. Seven months later, in February 1996, the removed paintings lay in the storerooms of the Russian ministry of culture awaiting restoration[161]. In July 2002, 43 works from the Grozny Museum of Fine Arts hung in Moscow at an exhibition of the Tretyakov Gallery[190].

T0122 Medical and Humanitarian Blockade
September 1994
C1193.T0122 →
C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996)
G0011 Russian Federation
S0010 Regular Army

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers did not let doctors and humanitarian aid reach the Chechens, and did not let the wounded out to the doctors.
Russian servicemen at the checkpoints around villages and towns surrounded before an assault did not let in doctors, UN and Red Cross staff, vehicles with food or buses for refugees. The occupiers did not let the Chechens they had wounded out to the doctors[138]. Russian soldiers fired on ambulances and vehicles of humanitarian organizations[138][191].
On 17 December 1994, Russian servicemen shot up a column of cars with refugees from Grozny near the border of Russian-controlled Ingushetia (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians"). The occupiers fired on ambulance doctors who were driving to the wounded from the Ingush side, and did not let them approach the site of the shooting until half past four in the morning[138].
In January 1995, Russian officials directed humanitarian aid to the northern districts of Ichkeria. To the south of Ichkeria and to Russian-controlled Dagestan, where Chechens had fled, Russian agencies sent no aid[177]. On 6 January, in Troitskaya, a stanitsa in Ingushetia, a soldier of a patrol of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs shot dead Ruslan, an unarmed driver from a column that a refugee woman from Grozny was leading there for the elderly (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")[183]. In early April 1995, Russian officials held up for a day at a checkpoint just across the border of Ichkeria a Red Cross convoy with medical supplies for Grozny, citing the fact that the drivers did not have the required documents[192].
On 7 April 1995, the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria. On 8 and 9 April, the special forces of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs at checkpoint No. 13 did not let into the village doctors of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), of Médecins Sans Frontières and of the Russian Red Cross[157][158]. Valery Borshchov, a deputy of the Russian parliament who was traveling to the village with the doctors on 8 April, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Moscow in February 1996: "As the major, the commander of the 13th post, explained…, they, the military, are guided not by the Geneva Conventions [international treaties on the protection of the wounded and of civilians in war], but by the orders of the local commander, Colonel General Kulikov"[161]. On 9 April, Dzeki Musayeva, born in 1920, died of a hypertensive attack without medical help[157]. On 10 April, Russian servicemen allowed the wounded to be taken out, but did not let ambulances into the village, and Chechens from Samashki drove 15 wounded fellow villagers to the post on a bus, a truck and a tractor with a trailer. Russian servicemen from positions on the Sunzha ridge, a range of hills near the village, fired on the trailer and wounded Taus Ibishev a second time; he died a few days later in a hospital in Ingushetia. Ambulance doctors took the rest of the wounded from the post to hospitals in Ingushetia. After this, the occupiers let ICRC vehicles into the village, and on 13 April doctors of the Russian Red Cross. The report of the Observer Mission of Russian human rights organizations says that at least 13 wounded Chechens from Samashki died because they did not receive medical help in time. The Mission published a list by name of those killed in the village, including those who died of their wounds without medical help[157][138].
On 30 September 1995, Russian Internal Troops and police surrounded Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria near the border with Ingushetia, and did not let UN staff with humanitarian aid reach the 3,000 refugees at the village resort, among them 2,100 children (see: "Transport Blockade")[138][193]. From 26 October, the soldiers did not let vehicles with food into Sernovodsk, and from November they let a truck with food in twice a week[138]. To the appeal of the representative of the UN Secretary-General of 7 November 1995 about the shortage of food among the refugees of Sernovodsk, the Russian government replied almost four months later, on 29 February 1996[177]. In December 1995, Russian servicemen fired on a Red Cross vehicle that was driving to Vedeno, a district center in the southeast of Ichkeria. The Red Cross staff could not come to terms with the occupiers and turned back[194].
On 14 December 1995, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Gudermes, the second-largest city of Ichkeria, east of Grozny, and on 19-20 December Russian troops captured it after five days of shelling and bombing (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[138]. The Russian government did not allow humanitarian organizations to evacuate Chechen civilians from the city, and the townspeople walked on foot to Russian-controlled Dagestan. On the way, refugees froze to death, among them at least four children[147]. In Osman-Yurt, a village in Dagestan, five-year-old Zali Zelimkhanova, who was walking with her family from Gudermes, died. On 21 January 1996, her mother Melkhash Zelimkhanova told human rights defenders of the international organization Human Rights Watch and of "Memorial" there: "When we were in the basement [in Gudermes] it was very cold, and by the time we got here my daughter, Zali, got sick and died a sudden death"[147]. After the capture of Gudermes, Russian servicemen for several days did not let ICRC staff into the city, while the elderly, women and children froze without food or water in the basements of destroyed houses. On 26 December, the ICRC began distributing aid in Gudermes[195].
In December 1995 and January 1996, soldiers at Russian checkpoints hardly ever let through the vehicles of the Belgian section of Médecins Sans Frontières, and the doctors could not get medicines to Gudermes[147]. On the eve of New Year 1996, Russian servicemen and officers of the Ministry of Internal Affairs at the posts around Sernovodsk beat the crews of vehicles that were bringing New Year presents to the children[153].
In 1996, Russian servicemen at the checkpoints checked humanitarian organizations for passes for travel around Ichkeria. Russian agencies issued a pass for two weeks, often a few days before it expired, or did not issue one at all[191]. By 3 January, the occupiers had closed the roads around Grozny and to Gudermes to ICRC vehicles. The commanders of the occupation troops in Grozny and the military leadership in Moscow did not reply until the end of January to the ICRC's requests to name someone to negotiate with[147]. On 5 March 1996, during the assault on Sernovodsk by the Russian units of Artemov, the commander of the occupation troops in the southwest of Ichkeria, the occupiers agreed with the ICRC to cease fire and let its staff through to the wounded and sick, but on 6 March the soldiers at the post did not let the ICRC vehicles through, saying that they had received no orders[153][138]. The Chechens wounded by the occupiers reached doctors only on 9 March, when Russian troops captured Sernovodsk[138], and the ICRC got into the village three weeks after the start of the assault on 3 March[153]. During the assault on Samashki, on 16 March 1996 the occupiers did not let through 17 buses of the International Organization for Migration, which had agreed with the Russian military to evacuate those who remained in the village, and did not let the wounded out through Novy Sharoy, a village to the south, although the Chechens offered 100 million rubles and a car for this[138][153]. On 19 March, when the occupiers opened the way out of Samashki, a doctor of the village hospital took the wounded to the hospital in Achkhoy-Martan, a district center in the west of Ichkeria[138].
In the spring of 1996, Russian troops surrounded the mountain villages of the Vedeno, Shatoy and Nozhay-Yurt districts in the south and southeast of Ichkeria. The soldiers did not let doctors or humanitarian organizations in[138]. On 10 July 1996, Russian troops surrounded Makhkety, a mountain village in the southeast of Ichkeria, and blocked the only road out of it, while soldiers at the Russian checkpoints around Shali, a town southeast of Grozny, did not let vehicles with the wounded through. Seriously wounded Chechens were carried out of Makhkety along mountain paths; four of them died of their wounds in the hospital in Shali[138].
The human rights defenders of Human Rights Watch wrote in their review for 1995 that Russian troops again and again blocked or delayed humanitarian aid to civilians in Ichkeria, especially at the start of the war, and at least once fired on a Médecins Sans Frontières vehicle with a clearly visible emblem of the organization[196]. On 26 March 1996, the UN Secretary-General wrote in a report to the Commission on Human Rights that, according to Human Rights Watch, Russian agencies created bureaucratic obstacles for aid organizations, hindered the distribution of aid and did not allow the sick and wounded to be evacuated from Grozny. Sergei Kovalyov, Russia's human rights commissioner, informed the UN that Russia was obstructing the delivery of humanitarian aid to the war zone, including medicines to save the wounded[177].
In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[145]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[152]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[138].

T0123 Deprivation of Drinking Water
September 1994
C1193.T0123 →
C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996)
G0011 Russian Federation
S0010 Regular Army

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers left Chechens without drinking water.
Russian pilots and artillerymen more than once destroyed substations and the water supply system in Grozny, the capital of Ichkeria, leaving the townspeople without water[161][185].
Russian servicemen fired from armored personnel carriers and helicopters at Chechens who were going for water (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[156][153].
On 31 January 1995, the occupiers shelled Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, from tanks and helicopters, leaving the Chechens in the village without water (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[157]. In February 1995, Russian artillery shelled and aircraft bombed Argun, a town east of Grozny. Chechens in Argun hid in basements and went out for water only between seven and nine in the morning, while the crews of Russian helicopters fired at passers-by in the streets[156].
During the assault on Grozny in February 1995, Russian servicemen in the Katayama settlement within the city limits shot 28-year-old Dzhenchuraeva with the cannon of an armored personnel carrier as she was carrying water.
